name: bezier-easing
role: CSS cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) as a pure easing function f(t), no runtime
summary: A dependency-free JavaScript function that turns CSS cubic-bezier control points into f(t), solved numerically. It owns no clock or timeline: a seeked canvas, WebGL or Node scene calls it with its own t. Its strength is reusing the exact curves of CSS, Material 3 and Carbon (published as cubic-bezier values) outside a browser transition, matching Chromium closely.
use_when: A published cubic-bezier curve (Material, Carbon, CSS keywords) driving canvas-2d or WebGL values from t
One curve shared by a CSS transition in a DOM scene and a seeked canvas layer
Over tween-js or anime-js when only the easing curve is wanted, not a tween engine
avoid_when: Springs, bounces or many-stop curves: motion or react-spring
DOM or SVG tweening with timelines: anime-js
Browser-only scenes where WAAPI easing strings already work: web-animations-api
notes: 2026-11-27: the lead's version, licence and install matched the npm registry (3.2.0, MIT).

assessment.rationale: npm 3.2.0 published 2026-10-07, MIT. Narrow but cheap: the motion pillar names cubic-bezier curves as its vocabulary, and no catalogue tool exposes them as a bare f(t). Overlaps tween-js easings only in part.

evidence.result: Six cubic-bezier curves, 101 samples each, vs Chromium 156.0.8078.4 WAAPI computed progress: max difference 5e-6 (all under the predeclared 0.002), endpoints 0 and 1, overshoot curve peak 1.098. Plot inspected; lines coincide.
evidence.scope: Four CSS keywords, M3 emphasized decelerate and one overshoot curve vs Chromium on macOS arm64, Node 22.19.0; not Firefox or WebKit, steps() or linear().
